The four forces of flight on an unmanned aerial system.

## The Four Forces of Flight
1

Lift

The controlled upward force created by the UAS's propellers, typically controlled remotely by the operator.

2

Weight

The downward pull of gravity on the UAS. This is the force that lift has to overcome for the drone to fly.

3

Thrust

The force that propels the UAS in a forward direction. This is also controlled remotely by the operator.

4

Drag

The atmosphere's resistance to the UAS's movement. The atmosphere is fluid, like water, so objects, such as UAS, must push around air molecules to move.

Beyond the Four Forces

Lift, weight, drag, and thrust are key forces that influence the upward, downward, and side-to-the-side movement of the UAS; however, additional factors also influence the flight of the UAS.

Drone pilots operating a drone for commercial purposes must maintain a Part 107 Pilot's License.

From the ground, a field may look healthy. But from above, drones can reveal: ![Stress Revealed](/WIAA/images/stress_revealed.jpg)

Drones are helpful at revealing information hidden to our eyes during scouting.

Why This Matters

From a top view, we can gain insights into plant health and field patterns that help us to understand our crop and how to best manage it. By viewing the field from above and using specialized sensors and software to calculate vegetation indices, we gain insights into plant health and field patterns, allowing us to better manage our crops.

1

Stressed areas in the field

Regions in the field may express stress in patterns that aren't visible from a ground perspective.

2

Cause of the stress

Diseases, pest damage, irrigation issues, or nutrient deficiencies often appear in patterns that give clues to the cause of the stress.

3

Impact of the stress

The extent of the problem can be used to inform treatment decisions and predict yield losses.

## Why Drones Matter in Agriculture Farmers and agriculturalists manage many tasks. Some require hand labor or equipment such as tractors. Others can be completed using drones. Drones can be useful for manual tasks such as spreading fertilizer or spraying pesticides. When a drone is equipped with a sensor, the drone system becomes useful for a wide variety of crop-scouting tasks — detecting pest outbreaks, estimating crop yield, or mapping field conditions. ## Drone Capabilities vs. Traditional Methods Understanding which tasks drones can perform helps farmers make informed technology decisions.

✕ Not Yet Drone-Capable

Tilling soil Crossing mungbeans Removing off-types Operating tractors and combines Fixing machinery Planting seeds in rows Harvesting crops Moving hay bales Collecting soil samples

✓ Drone-Capable Tasks

Detecting insect outbreaks Detecting disease outbreaks Scouting for weeds Mapping field terrain Detecting nutrient deficiencies Estimating crop yield Measuring plant height Checking emergence uniformity Mapping soil moisture Mapping soil texture Assessing storm damage Detecting water stress Monitoring crop growth
## Learning Activities
  • Categorize farming tasks based on whether they require manual labor, traditional equipment, drones, or a combination of technologies.
  • Identify which agricultural tasks in your region would benefit most from drone technology, and explain the advantages for each task.

Once you become a Part 107 Pilot, you must ensure the drone you plan to operate is registered with the FAA and is set up with a Remote ID or is only flown in a FAA-recognized Identification Area (FRIA).

Just like owning and driving a vehicle, drones must be registered and identifiable.

Once every three years any U.S. citizen or permanent resident above the age of 13 can register a drone for $5. The drone registration must be in the operator’s possession each time the drone is flown, and the drone must be labeled with the registration number.

## Remote ID Drones must also be equipped with a **Remote ID** which is a way for the drone to be identified by others by the detection of a signal broadcasted by the drone. This can work two ways:
1

Built-in Standard Remote ID

Broadcasts the drone's information for the entire duration of the mission.

2

Broadcast Module

An attached module thatbroadcasts information about the drone the entire duration of the mission but must occur within line-of sight of the pilot.

![Remote ID](/WIAA/images/remote_ID.jpg)

Remote identification options for drones.6

No Remote ID?

If a Remote ID is not built in or attached to the drone, the drone is limited to operations within a FAA-Recognized Identification Area FIRA. This area allows drones without identification broadcasted to still be operated, if the pilot and the drone are both within the FRIA zone and the drone is within line of sight of the pilot.

  • Propellers, landing gear, and camera
  • Radio signal between drone and controller
  • Current weather conditions
  • Mental and physical condition of the operator

Every image a drone captures gets tagged with a GPS position, but not all coordinate systems are equally precise for stitching data together.

## WGS84: The Default, With a Catch Drones typically record the GPS position of each image captured during flight. This is useful while stitching aligning the photos. However, often the coordinate systems are in WGS84, a global coordinate system that uses longitude, latitude, and elevation to determine image position

Why WGS84 Can Fall Short

The problem with using WGS84 during stitching is that the distance between degrees of longitude narrows as latitude moves from the equator. Because of the inconsistency in distance measurement, processing data with high precision requires a different solution.

## Projected Coordinate Systems The Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) use a grid system to project standardized measurements across the globe and provide highly precise positioning. ## Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) RTK tools use projected coordinate systems that use satellites to achieve highly precise positioning accuracy. Drones can be equipped with RTK systems to enhance the precision and accuracy recorded for each image captured.

During data collection and processing, researchers must ensure the coordinate system used by the drone matches the coordinate system used when recording GCP locations and any other positional data included in data processing and analysis.

## Uncontrolled Airspace This section of the national airspace is often part of **Class G airspace**, or uncontrolled airspace, where air traffic control (ATC) does not monitor or control the airspace. Class G airspace generally spans from the ground surface to 1,200 ft AGL where class E airspace begins. ## Controlled Airspace Above Class G airspace or across the country where ATC support is available is controlled airspace. Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace designate different areas of the airspace where aircraft travel. Airspace classes can vary based on context, but general airspace classifications are provided. Class B, C, and D typically begin at the ground surface and extend up to different heights depending on the air traffic surrounding airports and all have operational control towers.
A

Class A

Extends from 18,000 mean sea level (MSL) to flight level 600.

E

Class E

Fills the space between Class A, B, C, D, and G, and extends indefinitely above flight level 600.

B

Class B

Often extends to 10,000 ft MSL around the busiest airports. Stacked cylinders that widen at higher altitudes.

C

Class C

Typically extends up to 4,000 ft MSL, also in stacked cylinders.

D

Class D

Typically extends from around 2,500 ft MSL.

Special Use Airspace

**Special use airspace** exists over a variety of high importance or risk areas which often have limits on flight activity. Prohibited areas block aircraft entirely for security reasons. **Restricted areas** and **warning areas** impose flight regulations due to flight hazards however vary in that restricted areas are regulated by U.S. federal laws while warning areas occur off the U.S. coast and may be in domestic and/ or international waters. **Military Operation Areas** indicate areas and usage timings of military training, preventing interference with non-military air traffic. **Alert areas** indicate airspace with high traffic or other unusual airspace activity.

When using a drone to record data, pilots can use mission planning apps to help maintain consistency during the mission. ## What Shapes a Flight Plan The pilot should consider the qualities of the subject and the trait of interest and the level of detail required to extract meaningful data.
1

Altitude & Speed

In plant science, a drone pilot may need to fly at a lower altitude and speed to capture highly detailed data. Some fields may be very large, so a pilot may choose to fly at a higher altitude and at a quicker speed to cover the area quicker.

2

Terrain

The landscape of the field should also be considered. If the land is highly sloped, the flight plan should be set to adjust for major changes in altitude to ensure consistent height across the field.

3

Lighting

Missions flown for the purpose of collecting spectral imagery should be conducted around solar noon (between 10 am and 2 pm) with minimal or even cloud cover to ensure consistent lighting.

![Mission planning app interface for flying a drone](/WIAA/images/mission_planning_app.jpg)

Mission planning app interface for flying a drone.10

## Sensor, Battery, and Software Trade-offs The sensor attached to the UAV is an important factor to prioritize to ensure the sensor can maintain quality during the flight of the UAV. The capabilities of the UAV and flight planning software are a major determining factor for the flight.
1

Battery and Altitude

A UAV with a long-lasting battery can handle flying at a lower altitude for a longer timer, where a UAV with a shorter lasting batter would handle flying at a higher altitude for a shorter period better. Flight planning software often emphasizes adjusting the speed of the UAV, and the altitude of the flight.

2

Overlap

Front and side overlap of the imagery can be adjusted but is a trade-off between time and battery life available for the flight and the quality of the data needed for the target data.

3

Software

The pilot should consider the capabilities of the software that will be used to stitch, and extract the data captured by the sensor after the mission.

When GCPs are placed in the field, the GPS position of the GCP needs to be collected. These help to align the images captured during the flight to each other during stitching and enhance the alignment accuracy of the subjects captured in the imagery. GCPs can appear differently, many are simple with black and white squares that can be easily used to precisely pinpoint the same location during GPS point collection in the field and stitching the data later. Other GCPs can be customized to serve specific purposes relevant to diverse imagery-based research.

## Color Correction Color charts may be placed in the field to be used to calibrate the imagery to a specific known value. ![Color reference cards used for calibration](/WIAA/images/color_card.jpg)

Color chart for color correction used with RGB imagery.

Calibration panels can also be used to correct imagery back to a known value. ![Calibration panel used to correct drone imagery](/WIAA/images/calibration_pannel.jpg)

Calibration panel for radiometric correction used with multispectral imagery.

When It Matters Most

Color correction is especially useful to do for long flights where lighting conditions may change or when comparisons are wanted between flights conducted at different timepoints.

Some tasks in agriculture require hand labor or large equipment such as tractors. Other tasks can be completed using drones. ## From Manual Labor to Sensor Data Drones can be useful for some manual tasks such as broadcasting fertilizers or spraying pesticides. When a drone is equipped with a sensor, the drones can be useful for a wide variety of crop scouting tasks, such as detecting pest outbreaks, estimating crop yield, or mapping field conditions. Drones offer many benefits to people in agriculture and other domains, however, there is still room for improvement of drones in agriculture. Understanding the current capabilities of drones in agriculture can help researchers to target their research and development to interests and needs of stakeholders. ## SWOT: Drones in Agriculture

Strengths

  • Sensor data can be used to detect pests and disease symptoms early.
  • Decreases time and labor spent on manual data collection.
  • Decreases intra- and inter-rater variability.

Weaknesses

  • Payload capacities, limiting their use for large-scale applications.
  • Limitations in battery life restrict mission length and capacity.
  • Agronomic expertise and applicator certification are required for data interpretation and operation.

Opportunities

  • AI-assisted image analysis is automating pest and plant stress detection.
  • UAS can be included in integrated farming systems to allow rapid and in-field pest and stress management.

Threats

  • Replacing current infrastructure with UAS is expensive.
  • UAS operation requirements and certification limits user adoption.
  • Interpretability of data and processing software limits user adoption and accuracy of analysis.
## Case Study: Drones in Breeding Research A plant breeder is someone who addresses challenges to meet the needs of stakeholders. To do this, plant breeders screen many plant genotypes each year, which is time consuming, laborious, and subject to inter- and intra-rater variability. ![Iowa Mungbean Diversity Panel](/WIAA/images/IMDP.jpg)

The Iowa Mungbean Diversity Panel from a drone's perspective.

The Iowa Mungbean Diversity Panel, demonstrating the many plant genotypes a plant breeder screen to learn more about the genetics of the crop they work with. To decrease the workload of screening the genotypes in a breeding program, researchers can use UAS equipped with specialized sensors to take measurements from above, decreasing labor, time, and rater variability. ## Storm Damage Scenario

You're an agronomist in Iowa. A large hailstorm just went through and damaged the leaves on your crop. You need to figure out how much damage occurred to decide whether the crop is worth harvesting this year.

How could a drone help here?

A drone equipped with a camera or multispectral sensor can quickly cover the whole field and map the extent and severity of leaf damage — much faster than walking every row, and without missing patterns only visible from above.

What information could the drone collect?

Aerial images showing defoliation patterns, vegetation index values (to quantify how much healthy leaf area remains), and geolocated damage maps that show which parts of the field were hit hardest.

What decision might that information support?

Whether to replant, apply additional inputs to help the crop recover, file a crop insurance claim, or simply proceed to harvest if damage is minor — all decisions that depend on knowing the extent of damage quickly and accurately.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is like giving computers and machines a kind of smart brain so they can do tasks that usually need human thinking. ## AI Is Technology That Can:
  • Recognize patterns
  • Learn from examples
  • Make decisions
  • Process large amounts of information quickly
![The world of AI](/WIAA/images/world_of_AI.jpg)

The World of AI

## Why AI Matters for Farmers AI can help farmers identify the type of stress, determine its level and severity, and predict how that stress will act in the future.

Without AI

Farmer walks 500 acres = 10–20 hours of work

With AI

Drone captures 1,200 images, AI analyzes in seconds

## Types of AI

Machine Learning

AI that learns from many examples (data) with human supervision instead of being told every rule. For example, we show the computer lots of pictures of insects and provide labels for ‘pest’ or ‘beneficial,’ so the computer can learn patterns and identify pests on maize leaf.

Deep Learning

A type of machine learning that uses layers that can process and recognize patterns from unstructured data without human supervision (labels are provided in both deep learning and machine learning, but in deep learning features are not provided to computers).

Generative AI

Deep learning models that can create multimedia content, including text, images, sounds, and videos. A generative AI model is based on foundation models that are trained on expansive data and is treated as a “base brain” for many different tasks. For example, we use a generative AI model that can look at a picture and generate a clear explanation, such as “This is fall armyworm, a maize pest that eats leaves.”

Foundation Models

Very large generative AI models trained on vast amounts of data. Foundation models can perform a variety of tasks such as writing, answering questions, and understanding pictures. ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude are examples of foundation models. They are like one big ‘starter brain’ that can perform different tasks from the same model, such as writing a story about a farmer or explaining corn growth and different types of corn. Foundation models can use text or images or both. For example, instead of training from scratch, we start with a large foundation model that already understands language and images and fine-tune it on crop and insect data. For example, ChatGPT is a generative foundation model that is already trained on Image (insect) and text data (relevant details about insects). We can also connect the foundation model to Iowa-specific pest guides using a retrieval augmented generation pipeline, so when it answers about ‘a pest on a maize leaf,’ it gives advice that fits Iowa, not just anywhere in the world.

Agentic AI

AI systems that use foundation models to target a specific area as helpers. Agentic AI can help individuals learn new information, create plans and procedures, learn to use new tools, and even assist with performing tasks. For example, imagine an Agentic AI system for a farm. It watches for new images from the field, asks the foundation model what insect it sees, and then decides, based on whether it is a serious pest, whether to send an alert to the farmer’s phone or update a spray schedule. This whole pipeline that acts on its own is agentic AI.

## Multimodal Models Multimodal models are AI models that can work with multiple data types simultaneously, such as text, images, audio, and video. ![Multimodal AI models](/WIAA/images/multimodal_models.jpg)

An Example

A multimodal model can look at the picture of an insect on a maize leaf and read the question, ‘Is this a pest for maize crop?’, at the same time. It identifies the insect in the image, uses its knowledge about whether that insect harms maize, and then answers the question in text. In this example, the model uses two modalities, namely, image and text, to reach a conclusion.

![Insect identification example](/WIAA/images/insects.jpg)

AI can be used to help farmers to identify, classify, quantify, and predict pests.

The electromagnetic spectrum is the entire range of electromagnetic radiation. All objects with a temperature emit radiation at some frequency. Radiation is emitted at different wavelengths, where each wavelength is a specific point on the electromagnetic spectrum. Different wavelengths can be used to transmit messages, indicate stress, sterilize objects, and many other tasks. In plant science, researchers can use different ranges of wavelengths in a portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, called bands, to determine plant health, or detect early symptoms of stress.
## Spectral Resolution

Spectral resolution is a measurement of a sensor's ability to distinguish between different wavelengths of light. A sensor with a high spectral resolution, such as a hyperspectral camera can distinguish between many types of light, while a sensor with a low spectral resolution, such as an RGB camera, can only distinguish between a few wavelengths.

Drones can be equipped with various payloads or attachments that serve a purpose, often for data collection. Spectral sensors are a type of payload commonly attached to drones. Some of the most used sensors in agriculture are RGB cameras, multispectral cameras, hyperspectral cameras, thermal cameras, and LiDAR sensors. Each sensor can be used to collect different types of data at varying levels of spectral resolution. ## Some cameras are passive and some are active.
P

Passive Sensors

Passive sensors detect wavelengths detected from a source other than itself. RGB, multispectral, hyperspectral, and thermal cameras are examples of passive sensors.

A

Active Sensors

Active sensors emit their own wavelengths and then detect the same wavelength they produced. LiDAR sensors are active sensors.

RGB Camera

Like your phone camera, produce images that use red, green, and blue light reflectance. These sensors are commonly used on drones because they are inexpensive and can achieve high resolution. RGB cameras can be used to determine plant height, count plants or plant parts, differentiate crops from weeds, among other traits.1

Multispectral Camera

Typically consist of 6 to 10 sensors that detect light reflected from specific broad areas of the electromagnetic spectrum. Some multispectral cameras allow specific bands of interest to be chosen, but often multispectral cameras detect red, green, blue, red-edge, and near infrared wavelengths. Red-edge and near infrared wavelengths are used especially in plant science to determine plant health because chlorophyll has a peak reflectance in the near infrared portion of the electromagnetic spectrum and has a steep reflectance increase in the red-edge portion.1

Hyperspectral Camera

Sensors that detect light reflected from hundreds of narrow areas of the electromagnetic spectrum. The data from hyperspectral sensors can provide highly detailed information about the objects captured by the sensor. Because of the high spectral resolution, detailed information on plant health to the biochemical level can be extracted to indicate early symptoms of plant stress. Hyperspectral cameras do suffer the tradeoff between spectral and spatial resolution, as they have limited spatial resolution. These cameras also demand high power and require more detailed downstream data analysis.1

Thermal Camera

Measures the amount of light emitted from an object in the form of infrared radiation. Thermal data is useful to researchers because it can be used as an indicator of plant health. When a plant is stressed, photosynthesis and transpiration are often reduced, therefore resulting in warmer temperatures of the crop canopy. Practical usage of thermal cameras is limited by cost, sensor integration on drones, and need to correct for thermal emission by surrounding objects.1

LiDAR Sensor

Can be used to measure the distance between the object and the sensor. LiDAR sensors emit a laser that travels to an object, reflects off the object, and travels back to the LiDAR sensor. The resulting data from the sensor forms a point cloud, or many datapoint organized into a 3-dimentional space by X, Y, and Z coordinates. Plant height or biomass can be determined from LiDAR data, although require high amounts of data processing.1

When setting the camera parameters, researchers must consider the level of detail needed for the level of resolution needed. The ground sampling distance (GSD) is the amount of area represented by one pixel. For example, if one pixel has a GSD of 2 centimeters, this means one side of the pixel covers 4 square centimeters (2 cm * 2 cm = 4 square cm). Four parameters impact the GSD of an image. ![Ground Sampling Distance](/WIAA/images/gsd.jpg)

Ground sampling distance calculation visual.17

1

Height

The first is height. As the altitude of the sensor increases, a larger area is captured by each pixel. Because a larger area of the ground is covered, the spatial resolution of the image decreases because less detail can be extracted from the image.

2

Sensor Width

The sensor width is the size of the sensor inside the camera. A larger sensor increases the GSD by increasing the area on the sensor covered by each pixel, thereby reducing the spatial resolution.

3

Focal Length

The focal length also impacts the GSD. The focal length is the distance between the sensor and the focal point. A longer focal length decreases the field of view, which decreases the area needed to be covered by each pixel. This results in a higher spatial resolution, and images with finer details. If the focal length is doubled, then the area covered by each pixel is halved.

4

Image Width

The last factor is image width which refers to the number of pixels wide the output image is. When increased, the image width results in a decreased GSD. This works because a higher number of pixels will display more detail than fewer pixels covering the same area.

Drone imagery can be applied to different problems in agriculture. The specific problem is often dependent on the user. An agronomist who scouts a field to identify presence or patterns of stress will likely be interested in data analysis on a whole field level, while an agronomist who evaluates different crop varieties or treatments, will likely be interested in data analysis in many small plots to look at each plot individually. After completing the above processing steps, we can create borders around objects of interest, in this case field plots, to determine plots with high and low VIs. The VI calculated for each pixel will be averaged together with all pixels within a plot boundary. This average value will be the average VI for that plot. Orthomosaics and Indices

Orthomosaic images are created from overlapping the many photos taken during the drone mission and geometrically correcting them to create a single large image of an area. An index combines reflectance map values into vegetation index calculations.

## From Points to Surfaces Beyond X and Y coordinates, pixels can have Z coordinates, which can be used to produce elevation maps.
1

Point Cloud

Point clouds are produced by mapping the positions of each pixel in the image to create a 3D map. .

2

Mesh

These pixels are not connected to each other, but once they are connected, they form a mesh, or a 3d surface of the area of interest.

3

DSM

Because the pixels carry height values, together forming an elevation map also known as a Digital Surface Model.

![Digital Surface Model example](/WIAA/images/processing\_dsm.jpg)

A stitched DSM of a field.

## Field Analysis: Separating Canopy from Soil Once the images are stitched together, and we know their reflectance values are accurate, we may want to remove any parts of the image containing unneeded data. Agronomists studying crops are often interested in only the parts of the image that contain crops rather than soil or other non-crop plants.

Masking and Thresholding

Applying a mask and threshing the image allows us to take an image with many pixel values and transform it into an image with just two-pixel values, black and white. Determining which pixels are black and which are white depends on our threshold value, which can vary from drone flight to drone flight. Any value above a threshold value will become one color, while any pixels with a value below a threshold value will become the other color. The remaining pixels representing vegetation can then be overlapped with each spectral band to calculate VIs.

Once the field is flown, two things still need to happen before the imagery is trustworthy: aligning it to the real world, and correcting it for the light it was captured under. ## Ground Control Points

GCPs help align the images captured during the mission and match them with the field where they are representing. The black and white panels are set out, their GPS location is recorded, and then we fly the drone. When we are done flying, we use the ground control points when we process data to align the images in the field to their correct GPS location.

![Ground control points visible from close range](/WIAA/images/processing\_closeGCP.jpg)

A ground control point in a field.

![Ground control points as seen in the processing app](/WIAA/images/processing\_appGCP.jpg)

The GPS positions of ground control points in the corners of a field

## Coordinate Systems: UTM Zones

Why Not Just Use Latitude and Longitude?

Drones typically record the GPS position of each image captured during flight. This is useful while stitching aligning the photos. However, often the coordinate systems are in WGS84, a global coordinate system that uses longitude, latitude, and elevation to determine image position. The problem with using WGS84 during stitching is that the distance between degrees of longitude narrows as latitude moves from the equator. Because of the inconsistency in distance measurement, processing data with high precision requires a different solution. Projected coordinate systems such as the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) use a grid system to project standardized measurements across the globe and provide highly precise positioning. ## Spectral Corrections Not every image is captured under the same conditions. Sun angle, cloud cover, and sensor differences all change what a sensor records, even when the object of interest has not changed. To correct for these issues, we can use calibration panels with known values to adjust bands to their true value. ![Calibration reflectance panel](/WIAA/images/calibration\_pannel.jpg)

A spectral reflectance panel for correcting spectral imagery.

When we use a specialized sensor such as a multispectral camera, the camera detects how the object we are interested in reflects light across the electromagnetic spectrum. However, each time we use a sensor, the lighting conditions around it are different; the time of day, clouds in the sky, or surrounding objects can result in different light being detected by the sensor. To fix this, we calibrate the camera to adjust the reflectance values detected by the sensor, so they accurately reflect real-world conditions. Each band has a calibration coefficient that is used to align the values captured in the image to the true values. ![Calibration values in the processing software](/WIAA/images/processing\_calibration.jpg)

Images displaying reflectance of wavelengths captured by different spectral bands on a multispectral camera.19

Healthy vs. Stressed Reflectance

Plants that are healthier reflect more NIR light while stressed plants reflect less NIR light. Healthy plants also reflect less red light than stressed plants. Multispectral cameras are commonly used in plant science to detect red, green, and blue wavelengths like RGB cameras, however multispectral cameras also detect the wavelengths reflected by the plant in the red edge and near-infrared (NIR) portions of the electromagnetic spectrum. These two wavelengths interact with chlorophyll and can be used as an indicator of plant health and chlorophyll density. Multispectral cameras can be used to determine the health of a plant.

Satellites are purpose driven, meaning they are scientific tools built to help humans in a specific way. These satellite tools often serve multiple purposes because they are equipped with a variety of computers, sensors, communication, and power systems that all work together to achieve a product.
1

Communication

Satellites are used to transmit signals between devices on Earth. Phone calls, texts, internet connectivity, and television programming are a few of the primary ways satellites help us communicate. Ground stations on Earth transmit signals to satellites above. The satellites then take those signals and send signals back to Earth amplified across a wide area.

2

Navigation

Global positioning systems (GPS) assist navigation and enable precise positioning. These GPS enabled devices pick up signals from satellites orbiting Earth and calculate position, speed, and altitude, of devices on Earth based on the time delay between the GPS receiver and the satellite.

3

Weather and Earth Observation

Some satellites carry multiple tools and sensors. Weather satellites carry tools that can be used to detect visible light and infrared radiation from Earth and Earth's atmosphere, which can be used to continuously monitor weather and provide data to make weather forecasts. Data from satellites can be used to reveal information about Earth such as temperature, vegetation, and moisture which can be used for observing characteristics about Earth, and monitoring changes over time. Weather satellites are geostationary, meaning they orbit the Earth at the same rotation speed of Earth, thereby being fixed over the same spot on Earth.2

4

Security

Satellites equipped with high resolution sensors can be used to monitor and track changes across Earth and securely transmit military communications.

5

Agriculture

Vegetation reflects light differently depending on plant health. Satellite imagery can capture these wavelengths reflected by the plants and calculate spectral indices which provide proxy measurements of plant health. These plant health metrics help farmers with crop management on a large scale, picking up signals which are hard to identify when manually scouting the field.

Satellites can be classified based on multiple factors listed below.

Scale

  • Large satellites — many complex instruments on a single satellite. Only one satellite is available to collect data or transmit information.
  • Small satellites — many satellites working together to collect data or transmit information. These groups of satellites are referred to as artificial satellite constellations and can consist of a few satellites to thousands of satellites. These satellites together allow a short revisit time between satellite passes over a location.

Orbital Altitude and Type

  • Low earth orbit — Satellites are closer to Earth and typically have a polar or near-polar orbits. A satellite in a polar orbit pass directly over the north and south pole during each cycle. A satellite in a near-polar orbit follow a similar orbital pattern, however their orbit is slightly off-set from the north and south poles. The rotation is slightly offset, so the satellite will pass over all parts of the Earth over time. Satellites in these orbits will pass over the earth multiple times per day, visiting the same spot on the earth during the day and at night. The timing of the satellite passing over the equator occurs at the same time each day, putting the satellite in sun-synchronous orbit.
  • Medium earth orbit — Satellites are further distanced from Earth and orbit in a semi-synchronous or Molinia orbital pattern. A satellite in a Semi-synchronous orbit rotates in a near-polar orbit around the Earth at a speed that allows it to pass the equator at the same spot twice each day. GPS satellites use these types of orbits. Satellites in a Molniya orbit circle the Earth similarly to semi-synchronous orbits, however their orbit is off centered from the Earth, which causes the satellite to move at different speeds depending on their proximity to the Earth. When the satellite is closer to the Earth, it moves at a higher speed than when it is located at the far side of oval orbit. This orbit pattern is used for communication purposes near the poles.4
  • High earth orbit — Satellites are at an altitude about 22370 miles above Earth's surface. Satellites at this altitude rotate at the same speed as Earth and are considered in geostationary orbit. This type of orbit is useful for weather satellites.4

Ownership

  • Government Satellites — NASA, ESA, or others that often allow data to be freely used by the public.
  • Commercial satellites — privately owned and operated satellites with a variety of purposes. Often require payment to use satellite data.

The position of the satellite above the Earth and the angles between the satellite, object of interest, and the sun all impact the quality of the image captured and the area of coverage. The line of sight is the direction of the sensor to the object of interest.

Satellites positioned directly over the object of interest have their sensors positioned at nadir, or a 0° viewing angle. If the sensor is intended to be positioned at nadir, but it tilts out from nadir, the sensor becomes positioned at an off-nadir angle. The off-nadir angle is a measure of the distortion from the nadir angle and is calculated by the angle created between the nadir angle and the off-nadir angle.

Sensors may be purposefully positioned at an angle different from the nadir angle. The angle created between the line of sight and nadir form the satellite is the look angle. The between the line of sight and a line directly vertical or nadir to the object of interest is the incidence angle. Sensors that are positioned nadir result in images with high clarity, however, sensors that are positioned at an angle away from nadir result in images capturing the sides of objects of interest, covering larger areas, and increased temporal resolution.

Some of the many tasks farmers need to complete can be assisted by satellites and satellite imagery. Satellite imagery is an especially useful tool that can help farmers to identify stressed areas of their fields and help farmers to efficiently apply crop inputs such as water, nutrients, pest management techniques, or pesticides. Using tools such as satellites for precise applications is called precision agriculture, and can help farmers reduce cost, decrease pest resistance, and increase profitability.

Plant breeders use satellite imagery to develop cultivars suited to diverse environmental conditions. Temporal resolution refers to the frequency that a satellite passes over the same location. Landsat has a temporal resolution of 16 days, meaning a Landsat satellite will pass over the same location to capture imagery once every 16 days which can be helpful for tracking seasonal crop growth. Planet Labs's SkySats has an average constellation temporal resolution of 6 to 7 times per day, meaning of the 21 SkySats in orbit, 6-7 of the satellites will pass over the same spot. If a user wants to mitigate effects of different satellites and sensor calibrations, the individual satellites have an average temporal resolution of 4 to 5 days. This higher temporal resolution of the SkySats allows farmers to track daily changes in crop development. The temporal resolution of a satellite depends on the speed of the satellite, altitude above Earth, and number of satellites in orbit.

Temporal resolution is also impacted by orbit pattern or the route that the satellite travels around the Earth.

Spatial resolution is a measure of the area represented by each pixel in an image. Satellites equipped with cameras capture raster images. Most images are rasters, which refer to images that are composed of pixels. Each pixel in a satellite image represents a small area on the Earth. The amount of area that the pixel represents is referred to as the ground sampling distance (GSD). A satellite with a GSD of 30 meters means the reflectance values shown in the pixel represent the average reflectance values for a 30 by 30-meter area on the Earth's surface. Smaller GSD values indicate higher spatial resolution because a smaller ground area is represented by each pixel.

Drones often achieve higher spatial resolution than satellites, allowing for intensive field monitoring, however drones are limited by the area they can cover and require weather conditions conducive to flying. While satellites can cover vast areas of land, allowing analysis and comparisons across large scale areas in near unison, they face challenges with cloud cover during poor weather conditions. Certain wavelengths can penetrate cloud cover to help resolve this challenge.

Energy moves in waves and the length and frequency of the waves determines how the energy can be used. The electromagnetic spectrum is a way to visualize the types of energy.

We can look at portions of the electromagnetic spectrum as either specific measurements or ranges. Wavelengths are specific measurements, such as 450 nm while bands are regions of the electromagnetic spectrum where the strength of the signal from the electromagnetic spectrum peaks at a specific wavelength.

![Bands and wavelengths](/WIAA/images/bands_wavelengths.jpg)

Representation of bands and wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum.

Some longer wavelengths can be used for communication, like radio waves, some wavelengths can be used for heating or communication such as microwaves. Infrared waves can be used for heating or thermal detection. Shorter wavelengths such as ultraviolet light can be used for degradation of materials or sanitation. Similarly, Gamma Rays can be used for sterilization or astronomical research. X-ray wavelengths are often used for imaging or quality inspection of materials. These wavelengths are not easily detectable by humans unless assisted by specialized tools. A small section of the electromagnetic spectrum is detectible by humans and is referred to as visible light. This consists of red, green, and blue wavelengths and their combinations.

![The electromagnetic spectrum](/WIAA/images/electromagnetic_spectrum.jpg)

The electromagnetic spectrum and a representation of the wavelengths across the spectrum.

Shorter wavelengths have more energy than longer wavelengths. Every object can reflect, absorb, emit, or transmit light in different quantities, and the interaction of light with any object can tell us more about that object. When these wavelengths interact with an object, the energy carried by the wave is distributed by reflection, absorption, emittance, or transmittance. Energy that is absorbed by the object is converted into a new form. Snow is an example of an object that reflects visible light, which causes it to appear white because all wavelengths are reflected equally. When light interacts with snow, the incident radiation or the incoming radiation from the sun is modified only slightly as most of the energy is reflected, while only a small portion is absorbed and converted into heat. Dark objects such as asphalt appear black because the materials that compose asphalt absorb lots of light across the visible portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. Asphalt absorbs a lot of incident radiation, and the absorbed energy is re-emitted as thermal energy which has a longer wavelength than the incident radiation from the sun in the visible portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. Any object with a temperature emits light, although the visibility of the light to humans varies by the temperature of the object. Lightbulbs and rocks both emit light, however the light emitted by lightbulbs is visible to humans. Some objects such as glass allow light to pass through them or be transmitted. Sometimes when light is transmitted through an object, the material of the object bends the light as it passes through, such as in a prism, this is referred to as refraction. Light can interact with matter in a combination of these ways to create the diverse appearances of objects we experience each day. A blue coffee mug reflects mostly blue light while absorbing red and green light. A red tinted flower vase will let most light pass through but will reflect some red light while absorbing blue and green light. Asphalt will absorb lots of visible light and will emit light in the form of heat.

![Light interactions with objects](/WIAA/images/light_interactions.jpg)

Interactions of light with common objects. Red arrows indicate red light, blue arrows indicate blue light, green arrows indicate green light, white arrows indicate heat emitted, yellow arrows indicate heat generated by the object, and dark red arrows indicate near infrared radiation.

When looking at a plant, sometime the appearance of leaves can inform us about the plant's health. We can use specialized tools and math to help us to calculate indexes that can fine tune these plant health observations. Red-edge and near-infrared wavelengths are two wavelengths that provide additional information about plant health based on the amount of light that is reflected from the plant.

Sensors can be attached to satellites or drones to detect the light reflected by objects from the above perspective. Often these sensors can be used to detect a variety of light reflectance. Some sensors detect just three bands, some detect 6 bands, and others detect hundreds to thousands of bands. The more bands a sensor detects, the higher the spectral resolution.

The pixels that compose raster images store numerical values that correspond to the visible wavelength they represent. A 2-bit image would contain 4 values (2^2=4). likely consisting of white, light gray, dark gray, and black. An 8-bit image would contain 256 values (2^8=256). Higher bit numbers can detect more subtle variations in light reflectance.

Many satellites orbit the Earth above the clouds. This high perspective helps satellites to capture vast areas of the Earth; however, clouds can obstruct satellite imagery. Some wavelengths such as microwaves or radio waves can pass through clouds because they are longer than the water droplets that obstruct other wavelengths. Some astronomy tools use microwaves and radio waves to observe the universe because these wavelengths can pass through cloud cover. Some slightly shorter wavelengths such as near infrared or ultraviolet light can pass through less dense clouds. You can still get sunburn on cloudy days because ultraviolet light that causes sunburns can pass through clouds. Clouds often appear white. This is because the wavelengths of visible light are too short to pass through the water droplets in clouds so get reflected and scattered.

Clouds are not the only obstruction in the atmosphere that can impact satellite imagery. Water vapor, dust, and aerosols can exist in the atmosphere and block or scatter light. Water vapor or other atmospheric gases include ozone or methane which alter light movement. Dust includes air pollutants that block visibility and decrease clarity. Aerosols may include organic particles that get suspended in the atmosphere from forest fires or volcanoes. Sea salt is also a common aerosol which can become suspended from ocean waves. Known issues in satellite imagery can also be accounted for during image processing using models or indices that "remove" unwanted reflectance effects.

The sensor itself can also limit the impact of the resolution of data collected from sensors. Over time, the initial calibrations of the satellite may be altered due to space particle and environmental conditions. This can result in reduced sensitivity, distorted images, or total sensor failure. Often these issues can be prevented or recovered from regular calibration, and regular maintenance to prevent issues before they occur.

Data resolution is a tradeoff between the four types of resolution covered in this chapter. High temporal resolution requires higher orbits opposed to the lower orbits required for high spatial resolution. High temporal resolution also generates large quantities of data, like spectral and radiometric resolution. To maintain manageable data sizes, only one or two of these can be prioritized on satellites.

Satellites are more than just cameras floating in space. Satellites require a control center, protection system, power source, an orientation sensor, communication system, and then the sensor. The MySat Satellite Kit contains all of these components.24 ![The MySat Satellite Kit](/WIAA/images/mySat.jpg)

MySat satellite kit.24

The computer systems and clock work as the central control center. This acts as the brain of the satellite and controls all other parts of the satellite. The main onboard computer is the primary processor that manages software, controls sensors, and manages data. The auxiliary onboard computer is responsible for secondary satellite systems, and the clock is used to accurately record data timestamps.24

The control center and all other components are contained in the frame of the satellite. This helps to protect the satellite components from damage and provides a secure location to connect all components together. Satellites may also contain additional insulation or reflective features to prevent damage from extreme temperature fluctuations.24

Satellites in space need to be self-sufficient when it comes to power. Solar panels are a useful method used to convert solar energy into electrical energy. Once the electrical energy is converted, the battery stores the energy for when the solar energy is blocked from the satellite. The battery controller and voltage and current monitor regulate charging and tracks power usage.24

When data is collected, it is important to track the origin of the data. Data points such as time of data collection, coordinates of the satellite in space, orientation of the satellite and sensor, and movement of the satellite can be used to process and provide context to the collected data. The gyroscope and accelerometer are used to determine the orientation and movement of the sensor. Photosensors also help to determine the orientation of the satellite but do so using light positioning. The servo motor is a tool that can respond to the orientation of the satellite and adjust the satellite to the intended orientation.24

The central control center acts as the brain to coordinate satellite activities, however the communication system is vital for receiving and sending signals from ground stations on Earth which can impact the delegations sent out by the central control center. The radio transceiver sends and receives radio signals, and the antenna supports the transceiver to broadcast signals from the ground station.24

Finally, with all the features in place to control the satellite, the payload, or the primary data collection devices must also be included on the satellite. Payloads vary by satellite; many have cameras that capture images of Earth. Some light sensors specialize in certain wavelengths. Other environmental sensors may also be included on the satellite to measure factors such as temperature, humidity, or air pressure.24

Images captured by sensors on satellites are composed of pixels, and each pixel represents a spot on Earth's surface. Pixels are arranged in rows and columns and work together to visualize the specific area it represents. Phone cameras capture all pixels that comprise an image in a single shot, however, because satellites are constantly in motion, each pixel must be captured separately. The method of recording pixel values varies by sensor, but two common methods are push broom and whisk broom scanners. Hyperspectral sensors commonly rely on whisk broom and push broom scanners to capture data. RGB, multispectral, and thermal can also use whisk broom and push broom scanners, however, area array scanners, which capture the entire AOI in one shot are commonly used by RGB, multispectral, thermal, and some advanced hyperspectral sensors.

Whisk broom scanners systematically capture one pixel at a time, working across rows of pixels in one direction, and then working across the next row of pixels in the opposite direction. The back-and-forth motion of capturing pixels one at a time is like the back-and-forth motion of a whisk broom.

Push broom scanners can capture a full row of pixels at a time. Many scanners fire simultaneously to capture each row of pixels before moving to the next row. The single motion sweeping motion is like the pushing motion of a push broom.

One concern about satellite data is protections or privacy issues about imagery over certain locations. For example, some countries have expressed wanting control or restrictions over satellite data that is collected over their region. Sensitive areas such as military sites, borders, or agricultural areas are the primary locations of concern. Another argument is wealthier countries may have access to data inaccessible to poorer countries due to relative cost of data, internet access, or infrastructure availability for accessing and processing. Unequal access to data can be narrowed to a local scale, where a large corporation may view privately owned land using imagery inaccessible to local landowners due to cost or availability.

Space data ethics explored this further by examining how to handle data that can impact people globally. The same data from satellite imagery can be used by people of opposite parties for conflicting reasons.

Protections over the data accessed are also essential to consider. Free access to data can be used and shared without restrictions, however data from private companies often has restrictions over what the data can be used for, how the data can be used, and where or how the data and data findings can be shared.

Data sovereignty is the idea that a country, group, or person has rights over data concerning their own land. Outer space is a global common, no countries have ownership of outer space or the data collected from there. This means that data can be collected over any area of the world without restrictions. The combination of data sovereignty and outer space as a global common prompt the discussion of ethics surrounding these issues.

Sensors can be used to detect wavelengths throughout the electromagnetic spectrum. Different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum provide insight into characteristics of objects beyond what human eyes can perceive.

Multispectral cameras are commonly used in plant science to detect red, green, and blue wavelengths like RGB cameras, however multispectral cameras also detect the wavelengths reflected by the plant in the red edge and near-infrared (NIR) portions of the electromagnetic spectrum. These two wavelengths interact with chlorophyll and can be used as an indicator of plant health and chlorophyll density. Multispectral cameras can be used to determine the health of a plant.

Plants that are healthier reflect more NIR light while stressed plants reflect less NIR light. Healthy plants also reflect less red-edge light than stressed plants.34

![Vegetation reflectance curve](/WIAA/images/sat_reflectance.jpg)

Reflectance of portions of the electromagnetic spectrum typical for plants.34

Visually, we see many plants as green, so in the visible portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, plants will reflect more green light than blue or red light. Blue and red light will be absorbed by the plant. Chlorophyll absorbs light in the blue and red portions of the spectrum.

Moving towards longer wavelengths, the red edge portion of the spectrum illustrates an incline in plant reflectance. An unhealthy plant with low chlorophyll will absorb less red light and therefore reflect more red light. Chlorophyll does not absorb red-edge wavelengths, so a large amount is reflected by the plant. If a plant is reflecting more red light, the slope of the curve from red to red edge will be less steep. The steepness of the curve between these two areas is a key indicator of the amount of chlorophyll present in plant tissues which can be used to determine relative plant health.

The near-infrared portion of the electromagnetic spectrum can also be used to illustrate plant health. Chlorophyll does not absorb light in the near-infrared portion of the electromagnetic spectrum like the red edge portion. Near-infrared light does interact with other portions of the vegetative tissue such as cell walls, which reflect near-infrared light when healthy. Chlorophyll, cell walls and other components of the leaf internal structure reflect or absorb light depending on the health of the plant. Combined, these structures reflect more near-infrared light when healthy, and less near-infrared light when unhealthy.

Sensors detect different wavelengths of light which alone can inform scientists about the health of plants and characteristics of other objects. However, when wavelengths are combined mathematically to calculate a single value index for a pixel in an image, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of relative reflectance values and correct for unwanted effects.

Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)

One of the most used vegetation index formulas. Once calculated, a high NDVI signals healthy plants, while a low NDVI signals stressed plants. A very low NDVI value indicates no plants are present and is a sign of bare soil.

Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI)

Includes a blue wavelength which can be used to correct aerosol scattering. High EVI values indicate healthy plants, while low EVI values indicate stressed plants.

Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index (SAVI)

Used for analysis to account for soil present in analysis. The soil brightness factor L limits the impact of soil in vegetation analysis. High SAVI indicates dense and healthy vegetation, while low SAVI indicates bare soil or limited plant material.

Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI)

Includes green wavelengths in the calculation. This method is used to correct Rayleigh scattering. High GNDVI indicates healthy plants while low GNDVI indicates stressed plants.

Normalized Difference Red-Edge Index (NDRE)

Includes red edge which can be used to detect water related metrics. High NDRE indicates healthy plants while low NDRE indicates stressed plants.

Often researchers are interested in high spectral resolution, or many narrow bands in the electromagnetic spectrum, but achieving high spectral resolution is often not possible to achieve at the same time as a high spatial resolution.

Artificial intelligence, or AI, is like giving computers and machines a kind of smart brain so they can do tasks that usually need human thinking. It helps them to:

  • Recognize patterns
  • Learn from examples
  • Provide suggestions
  • Make decisions
![The world of AI](/WIAA/images/world_of_AI.jpg)

The AI Universe.

Artificial Intelligence

Smart computers that think like humans.

For example, we want a smart computer system that can use a human supplied image, which it uses to identify pests on maize and decide what to do (e.g., pest mitigation techniques, pest severity), helping farmers with decision making.

Machine Learning

AI that learns from many examples (data) with human supervision instead of being told every rule.

For example, we show the computer lots of pictures of insects and provide labels for "pest" or "beneficial," so the computer can learn patterns and identify pests on maize leaf.

Deep Learning

A type of machine learning that uses layers that can process and recognize patterns from unstructured data without human supervision (labels are provided in both deep learning and machine learning, but in deep learning features are not provided to computers).

For example, we use deep learning to enable the computer to detect fine details in insect pictures and recognize them accurately through pattern recognition without human supervision.

Generative AI

Deep learning models that can create multimedia content, including text, images, sounds, and videos. A generative AI model is based on foundation models that are trained on expansive data and is treated as a "base brain" for many different tasks.

For example, we use a generative AI model that can look at a picture and generate a clear explanation, such as "This is fall armyworm, a maize pest that eats leaves."

Foundation Models

Very large generative AI models trained on vast amounts of data. Foundation models can perform a variety of tasks such as writing, answering questions, and understanding pictures. ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude are examples of foundation models. They are like one big "starter brain" that can perform different tasks from the same model, such as writing a story about a farmer or explaining corn growth and different types of corn. Foundation models can use text or images or both.

For example, instead of training from scratch, we start with a large foundation model that already understands language and images and fine-tune it on crop and insect data. For example, ChatGPT is a generative foundation model that is already trained on Image (insect) and text data (relevant details about insects). We can also connect the foundation model to Iowa-specific pest guides using a retrieval augmented generation pipeline, so when it answers about "a pest on a maize leaf," it gives advice that fits Iowa, not just anywhere in the world.

Agentic AI

AI systems that use foundation models to target a specific area as helpers. Agentic AI can help individuals learn new information, create plans and procedures, learn to use new tools, and even assist with performing tasks.

For example, imagine an Agentic AI system for a farm. It watches for new images from the field, asks the foundation model what insect it sees, and then decides, based on whether it is a serious pest, whether to send an alert to the farmer's phone or update a spray schedule. This whole pipeline that acts on its own is agentic AI.

Satellite systems are equipped with different sensors that can provide information best suited for different applications. The resolution of sensors varies between different satellites. Some satellites provide high spatial resolution that can be used for detailed field analysis. Other satellites have more coarse spatial resolution; however, they have a higher temporal resolution that provides data more often. The spectral resolution is also an important consideration to ensure the imagery data can be used to extract information needed. Cost of accessing data also varies by satellite with some accessible freely, while others require either a one-time payment or annual subscriptions.

When requesting satellite data, the area of interest (AOI) must be defined spatially and temporally. Coordinates of AOI corners provide the area, while start and end dates of data acquisition provide a range of data to gather. Data over multiple times can be very useful and is highly reliable because of the satellite's consistent orbital pattern.

Once the images are stitched together, and we adjust for atmospheric effects and know they are positioned correctly, we may want to remove any part of the image that we are not interested in. In plant science, we may only be interested in the parts of the image that contain plants.

Masking and Thresholding

Applying a mask and threshing the image allows us to take an image with many pixel values and transform it into an image with just two-pixel values, black and white. Determining which pixels are black and which are white depends on our threshold value which can vary by satellite pass. Any value above a threshold value will become one color (black), while any pixels with a value below a threshold value will become the other value (white). Any pixel above the threshold value will be kept in the photo, while values below the threshold value will be removed. This technique is used to remove soil from images to prevent soil values from being included in analysis.

This allows AI to identify objects in images it has never seen before.
